title: Levers of Influence: Power Tools of the Trades
coreMove: Spot the trigger feature before you treat the yes as your own full judgment.
sourcePressure: The source centers automatic responding, fixed-action patterns, trigger features, click-run behavior, weak because-reasons, learned shortcuts, and contrast effects that skilled persuaders can exploit.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Do not write this as a broad warning that people are irrational; the point is the cue that launches an efficient response sequence.

hook: A yes can happen before thought
tryThisNow: Think more carefully for one minute
examples: teacher asks for homework because she said so

exampleSpecs.domain: airport standby desk during an oversold regional flight
exampleSpecs.audience: a traveler deciding whether to surrender a seat
exampleSpecs.stakes: missing a funeral connection versus accepting a voucher that sounds larger after a bad first offer
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the gate agent names the lowest voucher after first showing a worse hotel-only option, and the traveler catches the contrast effect before agreeing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a blue boarding pass bent around the traveler's thumb

exampleSpecs.domain: pharmacy counter with a refill authorization form
exampleSpecs.audience: a patient being asked to sign one more line
exampleSpecs.stakes: enrolling in a paid reminder program without noticing the cue that made signing automatic
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the clerk says because we keep your refills safe while sliding the paid-program form forward, and the patient points to the actual reason line before signing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a prescription bag stapled shut under clear tape

exampleSpecs.domain: farmers market honey stall with three jar sizes
exampleSpecs.audience: a shopper comparing prices under a striped canopy
exampleSpecs.stakes: buying the middle jar because the display makes it feel sensible
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the vendor places an oversized premium jar beside the normal jar and the shopper names the contrast before choosing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: sunlight through amber honey in a square jar

exampleSpecs.domain: museum membership kiosk after a special exhibit
exampleSpecs.audience: a visitor deciding at the exit counter
exampleSpecs.stakes: joining a tier because the suggested option is anchored beside a much costlier donor tier
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the visitor watches the clerk tap the top donor tier first, then asks to see the benefits without the anchor tier on screen
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a glossy exhibit wristband stuck to a coat sleeve

exampleSpecs.domain: bike repair counter during a brake-pad replacement
exampleSpecs.audience: a commuter approving a repair estimate
exampleSpecs.stakes: adding parts because the mechanic uses a technical cue that sounds like necessity
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the mechanic uses a jargon phrase, and the commuter asks which visible symptom proves each added part is needed
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a loose brake pad resting on an oil-stained invoice

exampleSpecs.domain: county clerk window for permit renewal
exampleSpecs.audience: a small vendor renewing a seasonal permit
exampleSpecs.stakes: paying an optional expedited fee because an official-looking stamp cues compliance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after paying, the vendor compares the receipt to the posted fee sheet and sees that the stamped add-on was optional
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a red stamp drying beside a stack of carbon forms

skillTargets: identify the specific trigger feature in a live request
distinguish useful shortcut from exploited shortcut
detect contrast effects in sequential offers
choose a response that asks for fuller information without overreacting

tryThisNowSpec: Look at the next form, menu, or offer in front of you and name the single cue that seems designed to make one option feel automatic.
